extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology, literary critics, and creative writers studying character and space in fiction
extracted.subtask_short: character and space analysis in fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing and constructing characters and narrative space in fiction, emphasising how textual devices (naming, description, focalization, repetition, semantic axes, genre expectations, etc.) produce the effect of character and space for readers. Useful for close reading, narratological analysis, and informed creative-writing choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on affective address rather than psychological diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis should not be about diagnosing characters as if they were real people, but about understanding how texts affectively address the reader on levels that approach unconscious preoccupations; returning to mythical referents is valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat characters as textual effects: ask how the narrative evokes reader responses and unconscious expectations rather than attempting clinical or biographical explanations. Example: read myths (e.g., Narcissus) to see culturally embedded clichés and prejudices that shape reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referential markers (names, pronouns) determine expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to a character (use of a name, a pronoun, an identity marker) constrains what the reader expects about gender, social status, origins, and behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to how a single mention (e.g., 'he', a proper name like 'Miss Marple' or 'Poirot') activates a network of conventional expectations; these may be used or subverted. Examples: 'Miss Marple' implies elderly unmarried lady stereotypes; 'Poirot' evokes a specific physical trait and cultural frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exterior description activates predictive frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical descriptors (age, attractiveness) and occupational details create expectations about likely events or behaviours in the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exterior description to either fulfil or frustrate expectations. Examples: a thatcher is likely to fall from a roof; a miner is likely to be trapped in a shaft. Recognize that mentioning these features creates expectations but does not determine outcomes absolutely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-bound expectations and their manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre conventions (e.g., detective fiction) establish outcome expectations (the detective must, in principle, solve the crime) and shape the type of tension in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how a text evokes, satisfies, or frustrates genre expectations; note how breaking genre rules shifts tension from outcome questions to character-determination questions. Example: The Locked Room breaks the detective convention by leaving mysteries unresolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader frame and reading behaviour shape predictability effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of a character's predictability depends on the reader's attitude toward literature and their reading habits (e.g., tendency to fill in details, speed of reading, frequency of interruptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider readerly dispositions when evaluating whether characterization feels predictable or surprising; different readers may experience the same cues differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse emergence of determination via relations to events
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about predictability provides clues only to potential determination; proper analysis traces how particular details relate to events and thereby produce determinations post hoc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between signalling predictability beforehand and explaining coherence after the fact: establish connections among traits, events, and outcomes to show how an image of the character is constructed through narrative development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition as a constructive principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of relevant character traits during the narrative strengthens and clarifies those traits in the reader's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track reiterated details and how frequency of mention consolidates the character image; repetition is a key device for constructing an identifiable character over the course of a text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation / piling up of data
rubrics_metrics.description: The accumulation of disparate characteristics causes odd facts to coalesce and complement one another, forming a coherent image of a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map how multiple small details (habits, quirks, background bits) accumulate into a gestalt; use accumulation to explain apparent consistencies or contradictions in a character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations with others and temporal self-relations
rubrics_metrics.description: A character's image is built through relations to other characters and to earlier phases of itself; similarities and contrasts in these relations are informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse parallels, contrasts, and reciprocal dynamics between characters, and the character's relation to past versions of itself (development, memory) to understand its constructed identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformations and changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters may undergo transformations that alter the configuration of characteristics; tracing these changes is fundamental to character analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the primary characteristics are identified, trace how events or internal processes change them and how those changes reconfigure relations and outcomes in the fabula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of relevant semantic axes
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose semantic axes (pairs of contrary meanings like rich–poor, man–woman, strong–weak) to focus analysis on the qualities that determine the image of the largest possible number of characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select axes that are widely applicable across characters; mark as 'strong' axes that are striking, exceptional, or linked to important events. Use chosen axes to map similarities/oppositions and produce diagrams of character relations; be aware that choice of axes reflects the analyst's ideological stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware binary-opposition reductionism; use degree and modality
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary oppositions reduce complexity and embed ideological bias; prefer sliding scales (degrees) and modalities (certainly, probably, perhaps) to capture nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace flat plus/minus dichotomies with graded scales and modal qualifiers to capture differences of degree and uncertainty (e.g., very strong → weakling; certainly → probably not). Use this refinement to avoid simplistic ideological projections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of markedness and detection of synonymous characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which characters are strongly or weakly marked by selected axes and map hierarchies; characters sharing identical axis values may be 'synonymous' and reveal duplications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create diagrams of qualifications (+, −, 0 or graded values) to visualise relational structures among characters and to expose inconspicuous duplications or equivalences in function/content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast descriptive qualifications with functional roles in the fabula
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the attributes derived from description with what characters actually do (their actions and roles in events) to learn about the story's construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how a character's described qualifications align or conflict with their functions (e.g., what actions they perform, what role they play in outcomes). Use such confrontation to understand causal or compositional relations between character and fabula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify sources of information and assess reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about a character can be explicit (self-report, reports by other characters, narrator statement) or implicit (inferred from actions); each source has implications for reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorise qualifications by source: self-analysis (may be unreliable), testimony of others (may be confronable), narrator commentary (may be ironic/unreliable), action-derived inferences (qualification by function). Note narrator reliability and examples (e.g., Dickensian ironic presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit vs implicit qualifications; potential vs realized actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit qualifications arise from direct statement; implicit qualifications arise from actions. Within action-based qualifications, distinguish between potential actions (plans) and realized actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat explicit qualifications as illuminating but potentially deceptive; evaluate implicit qualifications for their capacity to reveal lies or secrets. Mark the difference between plans (potential) and performed actions (realized) when assessing character commitment and transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight qualifications by multiplicity and frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: The more independent ways a qualification is communicated, and the more frequently it occurs, the greater the emphasis and plausibility of that qualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying characters, use number of sources and frequency of mentions in conjunction with numbers of semantic axes to produce a subtler classification beyond the old round/flat dichotomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be critical of one's analytic model to expose ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of axes and binary frameworks can project ideology onto texts; moving from uncritical projection to critical exposure of ideological tenets is a central goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constantly interrogate how your chosen categories and binary oppositions may reflect your own ideological assumptions; use the model both as a mode of projecting ideology and as a tool to reveal the text's ideological positions (e.g., sex linked to militarism in certain historic corpora).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat characters as textual constructions (avoid anthropomorphism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain distance from anthropomorphism: characters (e.g., Proust's Albertine) may be deliberately 'paper people' or 'flat' as an aesthetic strategy rather than psychologically deep individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret flatness or lack of 'depth' as potentially intentional and productive for the work's aesthetic and epistemological aims; avoid forcing realist/moralist readings that obscure narrative strategies and thwart appreciation of construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space as perception-linked and tied to focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Space in narrative is constituted by places seen in relation to their points of perception (a character's viewpoint or an anonymous/guide-like focalizer); spatial description is part of focalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how points of perception (characteral or external) shape spatial presentation. Examples: travelling gaze/travelling shot links character and space (Yonville in Madame Bovary); the travel-guide gaze naturalizes space and binds it to character understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural description connects discourse to fabula and naturalizes mimeis
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions generated by a character's manipulation of objects (procedural description) produce the emergence of objects and space for the reader, and can theatricalize or naturalize the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use procedural description to study how actions bring objects/places into text-world existence; examine whether representation functions as theatrical mise-en-scène (artificial) or as naturalizing mimicry of the real. Example: Zola’s L’assommoir beginning conjures women, laundry pit, crowd, and the bone of contention that structures the fabula.
